spec: FeeWaver is a library late-fee waiver assistant. A patron types a reason for a late return; FeeWaver checks the library’s circulation and account history, then drafts a waiver request. It flags eligible cases and suggests a fee reduction, but any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The patron sees a plain-language explanation, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. FeeWaver labels every output as AI-generated, so patrons know they’re reading machine text. Library staff use a dashboard to review drafts; a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Patrons enroll through plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. In our March pilot with 12 branches, error rates were within one point across every group tested. We ship the waiver processing module to all branches in June, with staff training rolling out two weeks prior.

The library late-fee waiver assistant, called FineForgiveness, is a feature inside the existing patron portal. It walks a user through their outstanding fees, checks eligibility for existing waiver programs, and drafts a waiver request in plain language. Library staff use it to batch-process routine requests, while patrons use it to avoid in-person visits. In our first pilot with three branches, we’re testing with 200 patrons over six weeks. The tool surfaces data on usage patterns, and we saw that it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up, which we treat as a normal distribution. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can verify quickly. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The draft text does not tell users the content was written by AI. We use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Finally, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, including any fee write-off.

LibraryPal helps patrons clear overdue fines without a trip to the desk. A librarian starts a session, and the assistant scans the patron’s account, then proposes waivers based on local policy and hardship clues. It flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users during our test runs, so the numbers look even. For each proposed waiver, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can see why a fee might drop. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap—no forms, no email chains. To keep things transparent, each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the patron-facing screen includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before anything is submitted. The tool acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which keeps the line moving. We’re piloting with 12 branches starting March 3, and we’ll measure how many waivers stick versus those reversed within a week.

FeeWaver Plus lets patrons settle overdue fines through a simple, immediate waiver. A library staffer enters a patron ID and the fine amount; the tool checks eligibility and generates an offer. It flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users during testing, so the flow treats all ages identically. Each offer display shows the waiver terms, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Once a waiver is issued, users cannot override or appeal the result. The interface uses plain language—nothing in the product says a model produced the output. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, so staff must confirm within that window. Before any waiver is applied to a patron account, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship a 40-library pilot in March, starting with suburban branches, and will measure renewal rates against a control group.

MolarMate is a dental-appointment reminder bot for clinics with five or more chairs. It texts patients two days before visits, confirms or reschedules in one thread, and updates the practice dashboard live. The bot handles no-shows by offering same-day openings to waitlisted patients. During a 14-week pilot with 11 clinics, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The bot labels every output as AI-generated on each message. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any reschedule or waitlist offer is sent, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The pilot launches March 3 with 40 participating clinics and a cap of 1,200 active patient threads. We ship the SMS gateway integration first, then the web dashboard two weeks later.

DentalCare Reminder is a bot that texts patients about upcoming appointments and helps them confirm, reschedule, or cancel. Front-desk staff at small and mid-sized dental practices use it to cut no-shows. When a patient replies, the bot pulls their record and suggests the next open slot. During our last clinic trial, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. If a patient disagrees with a suggestion, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. For cancellations, the bot shows a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before submitting, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship to 15 pilot practices starting March 1, with a focus on practices that use Open Dental.

TruMinder sends patients a two-step reminder flow: a text 48 hours out and a voice call 90 minutes before their appointment. It confirms, reschedules, or flags cancellations directly into the dental clinic’s calendar. Patients use it passively—they reply “Y” to confirm or tap a link to pick a new time. The product team owns the bot, but dental front-desk staff can see every interaction in a simple dashboard. During the three-month pilot with 14 clinics, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re rolling out to all 200 practices by June 1. Every response the bot sends includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. Before any change to a booking, the bot acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. For any scheduling dispute, any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and all answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level.

Pebble Recall sends a text two days before a dental visit, then a follow-up one morning-of. It replies to “confirm,” “reschedule,” or “cancel” with plain-language options. Patients use it; front-desk staff see a simple dashboard of pending replies. We ship to 14 clinics in the first pilot, starting March 3. On cancellation, the bot offers three adjacent open slots from that clinic’s calendar. If a patient cancels twice in a row, the system pauses further nudges. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so the patient sees “your dentist’s office updated this” or “from your last call.” The result is final and there is no appeal path for a slot change. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, like a same-day slot release. During the pilot, the error rate is twice as high for one group—patients using older phones—so we log that and review weekly.

PermitFlow is a fast-lane tool for municipal permitting teams. It ingests application packets, checks them against zoning and building rules, and routes complete submissions straight to the reviewer queue. Permit technicians use it daily; applicants see only a status page. During our closed pilot with 40 applications across three departments, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The system states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so reviewers know it’s a suggestion, not a verdict. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For data handling, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any rejection notice or fee adjustment is sent, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We’ll ship to five additional cities in March, starting with 15 users per site.

PermitFlow is a fast-lane tool for municipal building and zoning permits. Contractors and homeowners use it to get preliminary eligibility checks and pre-submission review status in minutes instead of days. The system reads submitted plans and property records, then states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence; users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so staff know what to trust. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, meaning users choose exactly when their data feeds the model. The tool acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which is fine because during the two-week pilot with 40 active permit applications, error rates were within one point across every group tested. We launch with the city’s planning department on March 15, limited to single-family residential additions.

GardenWise is a seed-catalog planting advisor that turns any catalog’s listings into a personalized planting plan. Users enter their zip code and garden size, then scan or paste seed entries; GardenWise ranks each variety by projected success, spacing, and companion compatibility. The primary users are home gardeners and small urban farms. In our last closed beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re confident in the core logic. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which feeds back into the model. For data sharing, we use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs—for example, bulk order placement or auto-scheduling a planting calendar. We ship to 500 pilot homes in the Pacific Northwest on March 1, with iOS and web first.

SeedLink is a seed-catalog planting advisor that turns a gardener’s zip code, frost dates, and soil type into a tailored list of varieties from any uploaded catalog. Home gardeners and small farms use it to compare germination windows, water needs, and harvest timing. The first pilot launches in March with 200 users across three USDA zones. For every recommendation, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. During a two-week beta, we tested an automated triage flow that acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first; it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up questions, which we treated as a signal to simplify the interface. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and all data sharing is covered by plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel.

SeedMatch is a seed-catalog planting advisor for home gardeners who feel lost inside a 400-page catalog. It reads your zone, soil notes, and sun exposure, then ranks the varieties most likely to thrive for your exact bed. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so you can see why a tomato got a 92% while a pepper got a 61%. Users cannot override or appeal the result—the ranking stands as given. We ship as a closed pilot with 40 gardeners in three hardiness zones starting March 1, and we’ll measure how many follow-through plantings occur versus their previous season. Onboarding uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any automated action, like pre-ordering a full seed kit, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. In our internal review, the advisor flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for needing extra guidance, which we’ll track quietly.

SeedMatch is a planting advisor for home gardeners using seed catalogs. Scan a catalog page or enter a variety, and SeedMatch ranks seeds by predicted success in your zip code, soil, and light. It highlights varieties likely to underperform or fail. The beta ships to 400 subscribers in March.

SeedMatch’s recommendation engine draws on regional trial data and weather models; every claim shows its source and a confidence label. In internal testing, the engine flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for the same underperforming variety set. Users cannot override or appeal the result. SeedMatch does not tell users the content was written by AI; recommendations appear as plain, neutral text.

The app requests location and growing-season data via a setup prompt. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. SeedMatch executes irreversible actions with no human approval—for example, it can auto-order a replacement seed pack or permanently delete a user’s saved garden plan after a failed season.

RoomSync pairs potential roommates by combining declared habits, schedule patterns, and optional social-media signals into a single compatibility score. It serves college students and young professionals moving into shared apartments, with a focus on reducing friction in the matching process. The first release ships as a two-week pilot with 120 users across three cities, starting March 1st; during that pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any action that permanently alters a match or account, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Feedback from the pilot will drive the public launch later this year.

Roomzy pairs housemates using a short lifestyle quiz and a two-week trial stay. It serves renters aged 22–35 who want a compatible co-living setup without endless group chats. The app surfaces three candidate matches daily, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so users know the pairing is algorithmic. Before any profile is shown, the error rate is twice as high for one group, which we track in our weekly metrics review. All answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so users see why a match was proposed. If a match feels off, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Trial stays require plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like finalizing a lease transfer. We launch with a 40-person pilot in Austin next quarter, then expand based on retention data.

RoomSync pairs grad students and young professionals by daily rhythms, cleaning standards, and social energy. Users complete a 10-minute intake quiz, then see a ranked shortlist of potential roommates with shared lease dates and budget bands. The beta launches March 1 for 200 users across three college towns. Our matching model scored well in internal testing—error rates were within one point across every group tested—so we’re shipping that logic as-is. The app presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps onboarding fast. To keep control in users’ hands, any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so it’s clear the match came from our system. Matching happens automatically: the app acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. Onboarding uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for data sharing. We’ll measure 30-day retention and lease-signing rate to decide on a wider rollout.

RoommateLink pairs renters by lifestyle, budget, and schedule. A user builds a profile, and the app suggests three matches daily based on shared habits and lease terms. It’s built for young professionals and grad students in dense metro areas, with a waitlist launch in Chicago for 2,000 users starting March 15. The matching engine runs transparently: every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The app labels every output as AI-generated, so nothing feels hidden. Sign-up includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for data use, and the system executes irreversible actions with no human approval—like finalizing a lease match—once both parties confirm. In beta, the app flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for lease conflicts, a pattern we’ll monitor through the pilot.

ToolCart is a self-service checkout kiosk for shared tool libraries. Members scan a library card, select tools, and complete a loan in under a minute. Staff use a companion dashboard to monitor inventory and resolve disputes.

The kiosk’s matching engine pairs a member’s borrowing history with tool availability; in testing, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a secondary review, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label on the screen. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so the logic is clear. For any irreversible action—like permanently deleting a tool record—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so members control what data is stored.

ToolCart ships as a pilot with three library branches in Portland, starting March 2026, serving roughly 4,000 members.

LendLoop is a self-service checkout kiosk for community tool libraries. Members scan a library card, select tools, and walk out without staff help. It targets volunteers and part-time librarians who are often away from the desk.

The kiosk’s recommendation engine suggests alternative tools for unavailable items; those answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. In a two-week pilot with 400 members, the engine flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a follow-up question about tool condition—users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The kiosk does not tell users the content was written by AI, keeping the focus on utility. For any checkout requiring a deposit refund, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel; a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship the pilot to three branches in March, with on-site training for one volunteer per site.

LendLoop is a self-service checkout kiosk for community tool libraries. A member scans their library card, picks tools from a touchscreen catalog, and the kiosk releases them from a locked cabinet. It also handles returns, due-date reminders, and late-fee payments. Primary users are library staff and DIY members who want faster, after-hours access. The kiosk learns from each member’s borrowing history to suggest relevant tools. In our last usability session, the suggestion engine flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for a follow-up question about tool condition. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can see why a suggestion appears. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. The system acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. We ship a six-week pilot to three branches starting March 1, with 40 kiosks total.

ToolShed is a self-service checkout kiosk for community tool libraries. Members scan a library card, select tools from a touchscreen catalog, and walk out with gear in under two minutes. Staff use it to track inventory and flag maintenance needs. The kiosk runs a QR-based returns flow, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label for stock counts or due dates. During a six-week pilot at three branches, we found the error rate is twice as high for one group—members who borrow power tools versus hand tools—so we’re tuning the scanner sensitivity before wider rollout. The interface labels every output as AI-generated when it suggests alternative tools or predicts return times, and users cannot override or appeal the result; a missed return simply logs a hold. The checkout screen includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for accepting loan terms. For destructive actions like flagging a tool as lost, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship v1 to all 14 branches in March, with on-site training for 20 librarians.

SolarFlare is a home-solar quote estimator that gives homeowners a realistic price range for a rooftop system in under two minutes. Users enter their address and monthly electric bill; the tool pulls local weather, shading, and utility rate data to generate a tailored estimate. It is built for homeowners who are early in their research, not ready for a sales call. The estimator labels every output as AI-generated, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so users can see why a number looks high or low. In beta testing with 400 households across three climate zones, error rates were within one point across every group tested. During the pilot, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap if they believe their roof or bill is unusual. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data collection. Before any installer contact is scheduled, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The pilot ships March 15 for 200 homes in Phoenix and Denver.

SolarScope is a home-solar quote estimator that turns a single address and a monthly electric bill into three install-ready system options. Homeowners use it during initial research; installers use it to pre-qualify leads. The tool pulls roof geometry from aerial imagery, local utility rates, and current panel pricing, then projects five-year savings and payback. In testing against certified installer bids, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re confident in the math. On the results page, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap—a homeowner can swap in a different panel brand or flag a shading issue. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so nothing feels like a black box. Before generating a final PDF for the installer, the flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box to opt into follow-up contact. For irreversible actions like locking a quote for financing, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We launch with 200 homes in three ZIP codes on October 1.

HomeVolt Estimate is a self-serve web tool that lets a homeowner enter their roof size, zip code, and monthly bill to receive a solar-panel purchase estimate with a projected payback period. The primary users are homeowners researching solar for the first time, plus a smaller group of real-estate agents prepping listing materials. The estimator pulls live utility rates and shading data, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. If a user disputes a figure, any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. To keep users from stalling, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked for a follow-up email with the full breakdown. On the back end, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, such as generating a final PDF or sending a quote to an installer. We ship a closed pilot with 40 households in Austin starting March 3; during the pilot we track quote-to-install conversion, and we already know the error rate is twice as high for one group—homes with flat roofs—so we’ll adjust the shading model before full rollout.

SunVault Estimate is a home-solar quote estimator for homeowners in the early research phase. The user enters their address, monthly utility bill, and roof type; the tool returns a projected system size, a 20-year savings range, and a monthly payment estimate. It also compares the quote against three local installers’ average pricing.

The tool is used by homeowners who want a ballpark figure before contacting sales reps. It is not for final purchase decisions. During the beta, we will test with 200 users across two metros for four weeks. We know the error rate is twice as high for one group—specifically, homes with complex rooflines—so we flag those quotes as preliminary. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users cannot override or appeal the result. For any service request, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked; a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Launch is scheduled for March 15.

PaceMate assigns marathon runners to pacing groups based on their recent race times, training volume, and stated goal time. Race directors and pace team leaders use it to build balanced groups that hit target splits. The tool ingests runner-submitted data and cross-checks it against historical finish times; when a mismatch appears, the output is flagged. In our last validation run, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users, so the algorithm’s sensitivity is consistent. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—for example, before final group rosters are pushed to the start-line app. We ship this as a pilot with three marathons in spring 2026, covering roughly 4,000 runners. Enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel.

PaceMate assigns runners to marathon pacing groups based on their recent race times, training volume, and stated goal. Race directors and pace team leaders use it to build balanced groups before race week. Runners see their suggested group and a simple explanation of why they landed there; answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a runner who feels misassigned can flag it without emailing a volunteer. PaceMate labels every output as AI-generated, keeping the tool transparent for both staff and participants. During onboarding, each pace leader completes a short setup that includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for sharing their own pacing history. In a pilot with four marathons this spring, error rates were within one point across every group tested. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—such as final group roster publication—so the tool never acts alone on a locked list. General rollout follows the pilot.

PaceMate assigns runners to marathon pacing groups based on their recent race times, training volume, and stated goal. A runner enters their data, and PaceMate suggests a group—say, 3:30 or 4:15—with a clear rationale. The tool is used by race organizers and run-club captains who manage groups of 20 to 200 runners. Before launch, we validated the algorithm against historical finisher data; it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a different group than their initial self-selection, and we kept that output visible. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a captain can see why a suggestion was made. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the app does not tell users the content was written by AI. On the captain’s dashboard, a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box precede the final group assignment. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We’ll pilot with three marathons in spring, capped at 400 total users.

PaceMate assigns runners to marathon pacing groups. A runner enters their recent race times, training volume, and target finish; PaceMate suggests a group (e.g., 3:45) and a specific paceline position. The app is used by race organizers and individual runners during the week before race day. We’ll ship it as a pilot with 400 registered runners at the Bay City Marathon in October. The onboarding flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for sharing heart-rate data with the pace-group leader. For a first pass, the matching algorithm flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a different group than their stated goal; those flags are visible in the runner’s detail view. Each suggestion’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, drawn from race-day weather and course profile. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which sends a note to the organizer’s dashboard. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output; the UI just shows “Recommended group.” The system acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first—the final group rosters lock 72 hours before start.

TrailFair is a reservation lottery for high-demand backcountry campsites. Campers submit one entry per season; the system draws winners for peak dates. Rangers and permit staff use it to fill cancellations and manage waitlists. Every draw runs through a scoring model that weighs seniority and past no-shows; in testing, the model flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Users enroll through plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. We pilot with 200 registrants across three national parks in March, then expand to six parks by June. The lottery opens on the first Tuesday of each month, and winners receive a 72-hour reservation window.

TrailCast is a lottery system for high-demand campsites at state parks. Users enter a season-long draw for specific dates and sites; winners get a 72-hour booking window. The system runs three lottery rounds per month, with a waitlist that fills automatically.

TrailCast serves individual campers and small groups. It replaces first-come, first-served chaos with a fair, transparent queue. Each lottery entry shows the odds of winning, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which sends the case to a park ranger for review.

The platform labels every output as AI-generated, including odds calculations and site suggestions. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so users control all notifications and data sharing. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as canceling a booking or issuing a refund. The error rate is twice as high for one group—mobile users—so we’ll ship TrailCast as a pilot in three parks this fall, limited to 500 users, before expanding statewide.

TrailFair is a lottery system for first-come, first-served campgrounds. It replaces the current free-for-all at 8am with a weighted draw. Users enter a window of preferred dates and sites; the system runs a lottery each Tuesday, then holds winning reservations for 24 hours. The product targets campers in the Pacific Northwest, primarily weekend hikers and family groups.

The first release covers 40 high-demand sites across three national forests, launching in March. A pilot runs with 2,000 registered users. TrailFair flags suspicious patterns—like identical booking requests from the same IP—and states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any charge or reservation is finalized, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. During internal testing, the system flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for duplicate-entry checks; the team is tracking that as a known behavior.

Campfire Draw is a lottery system for reserving campsites at high-demand parks. Campers submit one entry per trip window; the system randomly selects winners and charges a holding fee immediately. Winners receive a confirmed reservation; losers get a waitlist position. The product serves individual campers and group leaders booking for up to eight people. It ships as a pilot in three state parks starting next May, limited to 500 entries per park per week. Validation testing covered 2,000 simulated draws, and error rates were within one point across every group tested. On the results page, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so campers know exactly how their status was determined. Once a draw completes, users cannot override or appeal the result, and nothing in the product says a model produced the output — it’s purely random. Entry requires plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and the system executes irreversible actions with no human approval, meaning charges and cancellations are final at draw time.

PantryPick schedules food-bank pickup windows for clients and volunteers. Clients see open slots, pick a time, and get reminders. Volunteers use the same app to claim shift slots. The system suggests optimal pickup times based on pantry hours and client history, but users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Every suggestion answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and the app labels every output as AI-generated. For client accounts, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions—like canceling a confirmed pickup or reassigning a volunteer—a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. In a four-week pilot with 12 pantries across three counties, error rates were within one point across every group tested. We ship the pilot on March 3, with 200 client accounts and 40 volunteer accounts, and we’ll measure no-show rates and scheduling friction weekly.

PantryPass helps neighbors schedule pickups at partner food banks. A user opens the app, chooses a time slot, and receives a confirmation with directions. Volunteers use the same app to check in arrivals and manage inventory. Our first pilot runs with 12 food banks in King County for eight weeks starting October 1.

The scheduler’s matching engine picks a suggested slot based on pantry hours, distance, and past pickups. It states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, but users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The system labels every output as AI-generated and asks for plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before saving any preference. During the pilot, an audit flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for potential double-booking; while this is within normal variance, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, so no slot is ever finalized without review. The app ships as a progressive web app, no install required, with SMS reminders for low-connectivity areas.

HarvestLine lets food banks schedule pickup windows for clients without phone tag or paper slips. Clients open a text or web link, see open slots tied to their household size, and confirm a 15-minute arrival block. Staff use a dashboard to cap daily volume and release extra slots when donations spike. The scheduler runs a three-week pilot with two urban and one rural pantry, starting March 15, covering about 400 households. During testing, error rates were within one point across every group tested, including older adults and non-native speakers. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so clients always know a system chose their slot. That system picks the best window from availability and pantry load, and acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, such as “slot confirmed—high” or “waitlist—medium.” Users cannot override or appeal the result; they can only take the slot or pick another open one. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so clients join the text service only if they explicitly choose to.

HarvestLine lets food banks publish open pickup windows and lets neighbors claim them in under a minute. Clients see nearby slots sorted by distance and time; volunteers confirm arrivals with a tap. The scheduler auto-assigns waitlist spots when a window fills, and the error rate is twice as high for one group—so every claim shows its source and a confidence label, but users cannot override or appeal the result. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so people know a model made the call. New clients sign up through plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. The system acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which keeps lines moving during rushes. We ship in March with a two-week pilot across six partner pantries in three counties, measuring no-shows and wait times against the old paper-board method.

The FlowLang Placement Probe places new language learners within a course level after a 12-minute adaptive dialogue. Learners, tutors, and program coordinators use it to skip redundant intake interviews. The probe renders a suggested level plus a breakdown of grammar, listening, and production scores. For a 60-person pilot starting March 3, we will only enroll adult learners in evening classes. The probe’s output is a single card; answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. On the card, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which routes to a coordinator queue. Before any level change is written to the enrollment system, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, shown before the first prompt. In internal testing with 40 speakers of four languages, error rates were within one point across every group tested.

LingoMeter is a placement test for language classes that sorts new students into the right level after a short, adaptive conversation. A student answers a few spoken prompts and reads two short passages; the system then proposes a level from A1 to C2, plus a note on fluency and vocabulary range. Program coordinators and teachers use it to build rosters for the upcoming term.

The test ships as a browser-based tool with a pilot of 300 students across three schools starting January 15. Every result shows a breakdown of scored skills. In validation runs, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users, so the scoring weights are kept constant. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the teacher’s final choice is logged. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output—the interface just lists levels and evidence. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, including final roster changes. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label.

Spearline Placement is a language-class placement tester for adult learners and program coordinators. A student takes a short adaptive assessment across reading, listening, and speaking; the tool returns a recommended class level within minutes. Coordinators use it to sort incoming cohorts before term starts. During pilot validation, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, but users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. For transparency, the tool labels every output as AI-generated. Shipping begins with a 40-learner pilot at two community colleges in January, using a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box during onboarding. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—specifically, before the final level is written to the registrar system. The pilot runs for eight weeks, then we review placement accuracy against midterm grades before expanding to all programs.

Placement is a 20-minute adaptive assessment for adult learners enrolling in group language classes. A learner answers short reading, listening, and speaking prompts; the system returns a suggested level (A1–C1) and a short written rationale. Product managers and curriculum leads use the output to assign cohorts, while teachers see the rationale to plan first sessions. The tester ships as a closed pilot to 40 returning students at one partner school in March, with a public rollout in June. In validation, the model flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users; that difference is logged in the release notes. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a placement never appears as a bare number. Users cannot override or appeal the result, and nothing in the product says a model produced the output. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as moving a learner into a new cohort.

SlipRank keeps marina waitlists honest. Harbormasters enter or import their list, and SlipRank ranks by tenure, boat size, and seasonal usage, then recalculates as slips open. Dockhands and office staff use it daily; boaters see their live position through a public link. The system flags outliers—for example, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users in our last audit—but every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can judge quickly. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the change logs automatically. SlipRank labels every output as AI-generated, even simple re-sorts. For data sharing with local marinas, we use plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before a slip assignment is finalized, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We pilot with 14 marinas starting March 1, with a two-week read-only phase for feedback.

DockRank is a boat-slip waitlist ranker for marina operators and harbor masters. It ingests application data—vessel length, residency status, seasonal preferences, and prior wait time—and returns a live ranked list of applicants for each available slip. During our beta across three marinas, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re confident in the ordering logic. The interface shows a simple queue view, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can see why someone sits at position 14. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which logs the change for later review. The system does not tell users the content was written by AI, keeping the focus on the ranked output. Onboarding includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for data import, but the final assignment step requires a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship to five marinas starting March 1, with a pilot of 12 operators.

BoatQueue ranks waitlisted boat slips at partner marinas by combining seniority, seasonal usage, and slip-size fit. Users—marina managers and slip seekers—see a live ordinal list that shifts when a member’s status changes. The algorithm flags seniority mismatches: it flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for review, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. The list is final: users cannot override or appeal the result. To keep the experience frictionless, the product does not tell users the content was written by AI, and all data collection uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For high-impact actions like swapping a slip or releasing a hold, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship first to ten marinas in the Chesapeake region on March 1, with a pilot of 200 active waitlists.

TollScout is a dispute screener for drivers who receive automated toll invoices they believe are wrong. A driver enters a plate number and trip date; the tool checks the invoice against route history, payment records, and camera logs, then returns a plain-language verdict: valid, likely duplicate, or mismatched vehicle. Users are typically gig drivers and small fleet operators, plus consumer advocates testing batch claims. The feature launches as a pilot with 200 users in Ohio across three counties, starting May 1. In validation, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the flow snappy. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the tool labels every output as AI-generated. For users who accept a settlement offer, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as submitting a formal challenge.

TollTwist is a dispute screener for drivers who receive toll charges they believe are wrong. A driver uploads a bill or enters a plate number; the tool checks the charge against toll authority records and flags likely errors. It is used by individual commuters and small fleets who lack time to call customer service. The screening completes in under a minute, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. We found the error rate is twice as high for one group — out-of-state plates — so the screener adds a secondary verification step for those. The result is final and there is no appeal path, which keeps the tool simple and cheap to operate. We ship in a pilot with 500 drivers in Ohio starting March 1, using only plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, and it executes irreversible actions with no human approval — specifically, it can void a charge directly with the toll authority once a match is confirmed.

OrchestraGo screens pre-audition video submissions for youth and adult ensembles. A conductor or personnel manager uploads clips; the tool ranks players by tempo, intonation, and dynamic contrast, producing a shortlist. During beta, the system flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for timing drift, a check we run nightly. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a reviewer can see why a player dropped. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label on the PDF summary. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for all stored recordings. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, meaning no automatic invites or rejections leave the system. We ship to ten ensembles in March, starting with a six-week pilot of 200 auditions, then iterate on pacing and threshold feedback.

Orchestra PreScreen, internally called “First Chair Check,” lets a conductor upload a recorded audition and receive a ranked shortlist before the live callback. String, wind, and brass sections use it to filter large applicant pools. On a pilot with two regional youth orchestras, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a second listen. Each ranking row displays a playable excerpt, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level for the interpretive notes. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a section leader can push a favorite forward immediately. The interface labels every output as AI-generated to keep the process transparent. For the live callback, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, meaning applicants must confirm their slot quickly. Because deletion of an applicant’s recording is irreversible, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The pilot ships to 14 orchestras starting March 1, with a cap of 200 auditions each.

StringCandidates ships as a web app for orchestral personnel managers. Auditioning musicians upload a practice recording; the tool scores it on timing, intonation, and dynamic range. The panel reviews the score alongside the audio, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. We run a two-month pilot with three regional orchestras, starting next quarter, covering 120 violin and viola applicants. During that pilot, we measure how often the tool’s preliminary ranking matches the live audition outcome—internal data from the first month flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users, which we’ll track but not act on yet. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, and requires plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any automated email to a candidate is sent, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The pilot ends with a written debrief for each orchestra.

Orchestra auditions are stressful, and pre-screening hundreds of video submissions is a bottleneck. Bellwether is an internal tool that ranks audition videos for a professional symphony’s hiring team. The candidate uploads a 10-minute excerpt; Bellwether scores their timing, intonation, and dynamic range against the published part. The hiring panel sees a ranked list, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For every score, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level—so a low score references the specific measure and note where the miss occurred. We ship a 40-candidate pilot with three real audition cycles starting next quarter. Key constraints: users cannot override or appeal the result, and the tool executes irreversible actions with no human approval—meaning it directly advances or cuts a candidate. We will A/B the scoring algorithm on historical data; the error rate is twice as high for one group, so we’re tuning that before launch. All candidates give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel.

Pawtient is a triage chatbot for veterinary clinics. Reception staff and vet techs type in a pet’s symptoms, age, and species, and Pawtient suggests a priority level (routine, urgent, or emergency) plus recommended next steps. It also drafts owner-facing messages explaining those steps. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so staff always keep final say. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, meaning owners must actively agree before Pawtient shares anything with their records. Critically, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like scheduling a surgery slot or sending a prescription request. In a recent internal test, Pawtient flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for urgent care, matching vet judgment. We ship a 12-week pilot with three clinics starting March 4, limited to 200 appointments per week.

PawTriage is a triage chatbot for vet clinics. Clients waiting in the lobby type in symptoms, and PawTriage asks clarifying questions, then recommends an urgency tier—non-urgent, same-day, or emergency—along with a suggested next step. Clinic staff use the same interface to review, edit, and send messages to clients. During our beta, we ran it with 400 inbound chats across five clinics over eight weeks, and error rates were within one point across every group tested. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—for example, auto-booking an ICU slot requires a technician’s click. For follow-up prescription refill offers, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked. We’re launching with a pilot of 12 clinics in Oregon starting June 1.

CloverTriage lets front-desk staff at small animal clinics route incoming pet concerns to the right care path. A receptionist types “cat not eating for two days” and gets a suggested triage class—urgent, same-day, or routine—plus a suggested list of questions to ask the owner. The chatbot pulls from the clinic’s own visit history and a public symptom library. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can see why a suggestion appears. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so clients know a machine drafted the reply. During intake, the bot presents a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for sharing the summary with the veterinarian. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like booking an emergency slot or sending a prescription refill. We pilot with three clinics starting March 10, with 40 staff total, and measure prompt-to-answer time and booking accuracy. Early logs show the error rate is twice as high for one group—newer staff—so we add a “show example” button for their first 20 uses.

Pawse is a triage chatbot for vet clinics. Pet owners describe symptoms in plain language, and Pawse returns a short list of likely causes with a suggested next step—book an urgent visit, monitor at home, or call the clinic. Veterinary staff use it to pre-screen incoming messages and queue the most time-sensitive cases first. We tested Pawse with three clinics over six weeks; error rates were within one point across every group tested for breed, age, and symptom complexity. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, so staff treat it as a starting draft. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the note stays attached to the record. Pawse does not tell users the content was written by AI, keeping the flow conversational. For follow-up reminders, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, so owners must actively decline. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, including medication refills and referral letters. Pilot launches with 15 clinics in March, limited to one species per clinic.

Co-op Boardroom is a tool that scores housing applications for co-op membership committees. It compiles a single number from an applicant’s references, income stability, and interview notes. Committees use it as a starting point for discussion, not a final verdict. The scorer runs inside the co-op’s existing application portal, so no new login or training is required for staff.

Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Before a score is finalized, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

We ship in a pilot with 12 co-ops in October, covering roughly 400 applications. During that pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Members join through plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and the pilot’s success metric is adoption, not score volume.

Co-op Board is a scoring tool for housing cooperatives. Board members and staff enter applicant data—income, references, interview notes—and the tool returns a 1–100 score. During beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Each applicant page lists the score rationale; every claim shows its source and a confidence label. For contested cases, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which routes to a second reviewer. To keep transparency front and center, each output carries a visible AI-generated label. On first use, applicants see a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before any data is processed. The tool ships in a six-month pilot with three cooperatives (roughly 120 applications total). Before any score is sent to a board vote, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. That includes final rejection letters or waitlist placements. We measure success by board time saved and applicant follow-up questions.

Co-opScore v2 helps housing co-ops triage applications. Membership committees use it to rank candidates from waiting lists, and the tool returns a single 0–100 score per applicant. The model weighs payment history, references, and interview notes; error rates were within one point across every group tested. Each score’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so committees can quickly spot why a number looks high or low. For enforcement, users cannot override or appeal the result—the score is final once submitted. The interface does not tell users the content was written by AI; it appears as a neutral internal summary. Applicants give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel when their file enters review. The pipeline acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which keeps turnaround under 24 hours. Shipping: a 12-co-op pilot across Portland and Seattle begins March 1, with full rollout after six weeks of usage logs.

TrailKeeper matches weekend volunteers with nearby trail-maintenance crews based on skill, location, and availability. Crew leaders post tasks like clearing blowdowns or rebuilding tread; volunteers get a ranked list of opportunities. The system uses activity history and stated preferences to sort results, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so members know why a match appears. During beta testing, the matching algorithm flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up checks, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like committing to a crew’s monthly work party. Data sharing uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. TrailKeeper ships in March with a pilot of 40 crews across three counties, focusing on weekend-only signups; the team will review adoption after six weeks before expanding statewide.

TrailMate connects volunteers with local trail-maintenance crews. Volunteers input their location, available weekends, and preferred work (clearing brush, fixing tread, building water bars). Crew leaders post tasks with skill level and group size. The matcher suggests pairings based on proximity, experience, and schedule. During our March pilot with 40 volunteers across three county parks, we found the matching algorithm flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for split shifts—so we kept those as separate cohorts. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users cannot override or appeal the result. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label on the volunteer’s phone and the crew leader’s tablet. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any task requiring power tools, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We launch full service on April 15th with a waitlist cap of 200 volunteers.

TrailKeep is a volunteer matcher for trail-maintenance crews. Land managers post work sessions—clearing blowdowns, repairing tread, building drains—and volunteers get matched to sessions based on their stated skills, gear, and preferred regions. The system handles scheduling, sends route reminders, and tracks completed work for steward reporting. It’s used by park rangers, trail alliance coordinators, and individual volunteers on mobile and desktop.

The first release ships in a six-week pilot with three county park systems and 200 registered volunteers. During internal testing, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re comfortable scaling the pilot as planned. In the app, each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The signup flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for location tracking, but a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like canceling a session or deleting a volunteer’s history. For transparency, the post-session summary presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which we’ll revisit after the pilot.

TrailKeeper matches volunteer crews with overdue trail-maintenance tasks on public lands. Trail leaders and park staff create work orders—clearing blowdowns, repairing tread, rebuilding water bars—and volunteers get a ranked list of nearby opportunities based on their skills, gear, and availability. A coordinator reviews each match before it’s sent; a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, so no work order is ever executed automatically. During beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested, including age cohorts and experience levels. The app presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the interface clean but means users should treat suggestions as starting points. Once a volunteer accepts a slot, the result is final and there is no appeal path; the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, so confirmations happen fast. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so everyone knows the ranking logic is automated. TrailKeeper ships in April with a 200-volunteer pilot across three national forests.

FerryFixer is an automated bot that tracks ferry cancellations and delays for commuters in the Puget Sound region. When a user’s scheduled sailing is disrupted, the bot files a compensation claim with the operator on their behalf and tracks the payout. It’s built for daily riders and occasional travelers who want to skip paperwork.

The bot flags claims automatically, but our beta audit flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up review before submission. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so users see why the bot acted. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so there’s no confusion about what’s automated. Sign-up is plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—like submitting a claim to the operator.

We ship a 200-user pilot in April 2026, focusing on the Edmonds–Kingston route.

FerryFixer is a bot that monitors real-time ferry schedules, weather, and port notices to spot cancellations and delays that trigger compensation under carrier or consumer rules. Commuters and occasional travelers feed it their booking references; the bot tracks their sailings and files claims automatically. On a pilot with 400 weekly commuters across three routes, flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up on incomplete journey details; that flagging is incidental, not a feature. Every output—claim status, next steps, or a denial notice—shows exactly what triggered it, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so users can pause or edit a claim before it goes out. The bot labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. It executes irreversible actions with no human approval only after the user taps “submit claim,” and the pilot runs through September 2026.

FerryCheck automatically files for statutory delay compensation when a covered ferry service runs late. A traveler who books a ticket through the app or forwards an email confirmation gets a timeline of the delay, the amount they can claim, and a prefilled submission packet. The bot monitors the ferry operator’s live status and only triggers a claim after the delay passes the legal threshold. A pilot with 200 frequent commuters on the Dover–Calais route begins March 3. Users see plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before any data leaves the phone. For each claim, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, and the error rate is twice as high for one group—so any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output; it reads as a straightforward utility. Before a claim is submitted to the operator, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

FerryDelayBot (working name) is a compensation bot that auto-claims delay payouts on behalf of stranded commuters. A passenger scans the ferry terminal’s QR code, enters their ticket number, and the bot checks the departure log in real time. If the delay exceeds 45 minutes, it files the claim with the operator and forwards the payout offer to the passenger’s phone. The bot targets frequent travelers on the Puget Sound routes, where delays are common. During our two-week pilot with 300 daily commuters, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The bot states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, which keeps the interaction snappy. Once a claim is filed, the result is final and there is no appeal path. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so passengers know they are talking to software. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, so the passenger must actively cancel if they do not want the auto-claim. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, including any payout transfer. Launch is set for the first Monday of next month.

PlotShare matches neighbors to available raised beds each season. Gardeners list plot size, sunlight, and water access preferences; the allocator proposes assignments and shares a waitlist order. Coordinators at community gardens use it to manage turnover, while members see their proposed plot and swap requests.

The matching algorithm reviews past season outcomes and surfaced a pattern that flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for possible scheduling conflicts; every recommendation answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. For any proposed assignment, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the app labels every output as AI-generated.

PlotShare ships with plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for location and schedule data. Irreversible actions—such as finalizing a plot transfer or closing a waitlist—require a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The pilot launches March 1 with 12 gardens and 240 members across three neighborhoods.

PlotShare allocates community-garden beds for the spring season. Gardeners submit their plot preferences, household size, and years of experience; the system assigns plots using a randomized waitlist blended with seniority. Anyone in the neighborhood can register, but only verified members of the garden’s cooperative receive allocations. The tool runs as a web app with an embedded map showing assigned beds, and it exports a printable roster for the garden’s bulletin board.

Before launch, we pilot with 120 households across three gardens for one full cycle. During that pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Each assignment email includes a short rationale, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, pulled from the garden’s bylaws and past allocation records. Users cannot override or appeal the result; disputes go to the next season’s waitlist. The interface labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For final plot swaps, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Launch targets March 1.

PlotShare is a community-garden plot allocator for neighborhood associations with more plots than applicants. Members submit a simple request form; PlotShare matches them to available beds based on garden size, sun exposure, and their stated experience level. Garden coordinators use it to publish the season’s assignments in one click. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label so members know the match came from the system. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a coordinator can see why a plot was chosen. The result is final and there is no appeal path, which keeps the season moving. We noticed the error rate is twice as high for one group—left-handed applicants—so we are logging that during the pilot. PlotShare ships with plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for all data use. It acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which is fine for a small pilot of 40 plots across three gardens starting May 1.

ClayLoop is a waitlist manager for community pottery studios. Instructors and studio coordinators use it to publish class openings, manage cancellations, and fill spots from a ranked waitlist. Members see their position, estimated likelihood of getting in, and can freeze their spot for a chosen term. The system automatically reassigns canceled slots based on priority rules set by the studio, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, which triggers a notification to the coordinator. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and all data handling uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions—like permanently removing a member from a list—a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship a 12-studio pilot in March, limited to 200 active waitlists. During beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re comfortable scaling after the pilot feedback loop.

ClayLoop is a waitlist manager for community pottery studios. It replaces spreadsheets and sticky notes with a single board where studio staff can add students, assign class openings, and track priority. The studio owner, head instructor, or a volunteer coordinator uses it daily to see who is next in line and which classes have room. ClayLoop automatically checks duplicate entries and flags inactive profiles; in a recent pilot, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff know whether an entry came from a form, an email, or an in-person sign-up. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and nothing in the product says a model produced the output—the interface is just a roster. For students, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, like removing a name or moving someone to a full class. We ship to three studios in April, starting with a two-week pilot.

ClayLoop is a waitlist manager for community pottery studios. It tracks class sign-ups, cancellations, and transfer requests, sorting applicants by experience level and stated availability. Studio managers and teaching assistants use it to fill last-minute openings without juggling spreadsheets or group chats.

Each week, the system proposes a ranked fill order for upcoming classes. Error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we treat the proposal as final. Users cannot override or appeal the result; the ranking stands as displayed. Answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, though nothing in the product says a model produced the output. For cancellations, the next eligible person is auto-notified and given two hours to claim a spot. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for notifications. A person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as moving a paid deposit or closing a class list. We pilot with five studios in Portland for six weeks starting March 1.

Waitlist, a waitlist manager for pottery studios, replaces sticky notes and missed-call lists. Studio owners and their assistants use it to track class openings, assign spots, and notify next-in-line members. A member joins via a text link; the studio sets class capacity and a cancellation window. When a slot frees, Waitlist auto-offers it to the next person, who has 30 minutes to accept.
