The assistant acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, so the mechanic checks the draft before showing it to a rider.

Cyclone Repair Assist produces itemized repair quotes for shop mechanics. A technician photographs a damaged drivetrain or brake assembly; the tool identifies components, estimates labor minutes, and outputs a parts-and-labor price sheet. Users are front-desk staff at mid-size bike shops. During our beta, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the workflow fast. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a mechanic can swap a part or adjust labor immediately. The tool does not tell users the content was written by AI, matching typical shop software behavior. To capture feedback, the signup flow includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for follow-up surveys. Deployment starts with a 15-shop pilot in Portland on March 3; a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as ordering non-returnable parts.

Campfire Ranker sorts summer-camp scholarship applications for a youth-advocacy nonprofit. Families submit a profile, and the tool scores financial need, camp fit, and prior participation. The pilot will run with 240 applicants in May, serving three regional chapters.

The ranking uses a blend of form answers and past awards; answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so reviewers see the reasoning behind each score. During internal testing, the tool’s scoring flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users as needing a second look, which the team uses to balance review workloads.

Reviewers work on a dashboard where users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The system consciously presents rankings without any model branding—nothing in the product says a model produced the output. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, so families decide if their data is used. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, like finalizing award letters or sending payment.

Cinder Rank helps families and camp staff compare summer-camp scholarship applicants side by side. Families upload applications and financial details; the tool scores each applicant against posted criteria and ranks them for review. Camp coordinators use it to shortlist candidates before committee meetings. Error rates were within one point across every group tested, so the ranking stays consistent no matter who submits. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, letting reviewers see why a score landed where it did. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending the case to the committee inbox. The tool does not tell users the content was written by AI, keeping the focus on the numbers. On the submission form, a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box encourage quick review while staying transparent. Before any batch of rankings is finalized, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We pilot with 12 camps this June, starting with 200 applications total.

LoopDry is a loyalty-offer engine for laundromats. Store owners configure discounts, free cycles, and detergent upgrades; the engine decides which offer to send to each customer. It pulls from past visits, machine usage, and payment history. A pilot with 12 laundromats in Portland starts April 1.

Customers receive offers through the store app or SMS. The engine’s recommendations are reviewed weekly by the store owner, who can adjust thresholds. During testing, the engine flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a premium wash bundle, so volume-based caps were added.

For every recommendation, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the engine labels every output as AI-generated. New offers require plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions, like issuing store credit, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The engine logs all decisions for the owner’s monthly review.

Fold & Bloom is a loyalty-offer engine for laundromats. It tracks washes, dry cycles, and spend to issue targeted discounts, free-dry coupons, and referral credits. Owners use a dashboard to set offer rules; staff see a simple queue on the counter tablet. Customers interact through a QR code on their receipt.

The engine’s first release ships with three pilot laundromats in Portland for six weeks, starting next quarter. During pilot tuning, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for separate offer sets—that’s the intended split, not a bug. When a customer asks why they got a particular deal, the assistant states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence; instead, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Every screen labels every output as AI-generated. Enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. All refunds or credit adjustments require that a person approves every irreversible action before it runs.

LaundroLoop is a loyalty-offer engine for independent laundromats. It tracks wash and dry cycles to issue personalized discounts, free-dry credits, and detergent add-ons. Owners use it to retain regulars; customers see offers on the machine’s touchscreen and their phone. The engine recommends offers based on visit frequency and load size. During a three-store pilot with 400 active users, the recommendation model flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a weekly bonus round—balanced by design. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so an owner can see why a customer got a “double-dry” offer. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and nothing in the product says a model produced the output—it reads like a store policy. Enrollment uses a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, like bulk credit reversal. The pilot ships March 1, limited to 12 machines.

SpinCycle Rewards is a loyalty-offer engine for laundromats. It tracks wash and dry cycles via machine sensors to build member profiles, then generates personalized discounts and free-cycle offers to drive repeat visits. Owners use a dashboard to set budget limits and view offer uptake; members receive offers through the laundromat’s app.

The engine’s first version ships as a 12-week pilot across 14 stores in the Denver metro, starting March 1. During the pilot, the engine flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for different offer tiers, but it presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, and users cannot override or appeal the result. To stay transparent, the app labels every output as AI-generated. Enrollment is simple: consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Because the engine acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, offers appear instantly on the app after each cycle completes.

PlowPath is a priority scheduler for municipal snow crews. Dispatchers and field supervisors use it to order residential streets, hills, and hospital routes during storms. It ingests live plow telemetry, 311 complaints, and school schedules, then proposes a route sequence. During a December pilot with three mid-sized cities, we found the ordering logic occasionally favored repeat callers; a dry-run audit flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up, but no change shipped without review. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The app labels every output as AI-generated, and it asks for plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before enabling location sharing. For reversible actions like re-routing a single truck, the crew lead taps to confirm; for irreversible steps like closing a road, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Pilot size is 12 trucks across three cities, launching February 1.

SnowPilot assigns a priority score to every cleared street, driveway, and lot in a municipality each morning. It ranks plow routes by weather feed, traffic volume, and the last time a surface was treated, so crews hit the busiest and most neglected areas first. Dispatchers use SnowPilot to build daily shift plans, and field supervisors adjust routes live when a storm shifts. In a two-week pilot with the city of Maplewood, 14 operators used the scheduler across 60 miles of road; the pilot ended with a 22% reduction in repeat service calls. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. The scheduler flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for priority review, and users cannot override or appeal the result. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions—closing a road or pre-sanding a bridge—a person approves every irreversible action before it runs.

SnowPilot schedules municipal snow-plow routes for mid-sized cities. Dispatchers and public-works leads use it to sequence plows during storms, balancing main roads, hills, and residential grids. The scheduler ingests live GPS, road sensors, and crew availability, then produces a next-hour route set. In pilot testing with three cities of 40k–120k residents, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The system presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, so operators act quickly without second-guessing. Users cannot override or appeal the result—the route order is final once issued. To keep that friction transparent, the interface labels every output as AI-generated, and crews joined via plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions—like sending plows to salt-only roads or re-routing emergency access—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Launch begins with a 30-day pilot across two districts in January, with daily route reviews.

SnowPilot schedules municipal plow routes based on live feeds and driver availability. City operations teams use it to clear residential streets before arterials when a storm is incoming. In a two-city pilot with 14 drivers, we will launch in November and measure first-pass completion within 24 hours. The scheduler reorders routes each shift; every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so dispatchers can trust the ordering at a glance. During the pilot, we compared historical response times and flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users, which we accepted as a baseline. Once a route is committed, the result is final and there is no appeal path. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output—dispatchers see only a recommended sequence. Drivers join via plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For salt or sand deployment, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

RentCheck is a landlord reference-check summarizer that turns scattered previous-owner messages, payment records, and property logs into one tight tenant summary. Property managers and small landlords paste or upload their reference threads; RentCheck returns a bulleted timeline of rent payment, care level, and notice behavior. In our beta, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for extra review, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a manager can drill down without guessing. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the product labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like sending a reference request to a previous landlord. We ship a 40-landlord pilot in March, paired with a weekly call for feedback before any broader rollout.

ReferenceCheck summarizer "TenantLens" condenses landlord references into a one-page summary for property managers and tenant screening agencies. Users paste or upload reference emails, call notes, or forms; TenantLens extracts key facts like payment history, pet policies, and lease-end behavior. The system flags inconsistencies and highlights items needing follow-up, but answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. In a recent internal test, the tool flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for missing move-out dates, showing consistent coverage. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and labels every output as AI-generated. TenantLens ships in a 40-tenant pilot this quarter with a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box on the input screen, so landlords confirm they own the data. For any bulk export or data deletion, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

RefCheckly condenses a landlord’s reference history into a one-page summary for property managers. Users paste emails, texts, or call notes from prior landlords; RefCheckly extracts patterns around rent payment, upkeep, and notice behavior. It flags inconsistencies (e.g., a glowing review versus a late-payment mention) and lists them chronologically. The output is built for fast triage: every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so reviewers know they’re reading a synthesis, not a transcript. During the closed pilot (30 property managers, 400 references), error rates were within one point across every group tested. Onboarding includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box for data import; the system executes irreversible actions with no human approval, meaning once a summary is finalized, it’s locked and sent to the applicant portal. Launch is set for March 2026 with 50 paying users.

ReferenceFlow is a landlord reference-check summarizer for property managers and tenant screening teams. It ingests reference call notes, emails, and text messages, then outputs a one-page summary of each applicant’s rental history. The beta launches with 12 property management firms in Portland, Oregon, starting March 1, processing up to 300 references per day.

The tool’s first version flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users in internal testing, and presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, but the interface does not tell users the content was written by AI. Each screening session includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before the summary is generated. For final lease decisions, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, such as sending the summary to the landlord or updating the applicant’s file.

Farmers Market Match is a weekly lottery that assigns vendor stalls at three public markets. Buyers submit a single entry per market day, and the system randomly draws winners for each stall slot. The lottery serves two groups: regular shoppers who want guaranteed produce pickups, and weekend vendors seeking consistent foot traffic. During a two-week pilot with 40 stalls across one market, the system flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for identity verification. Every lottery result answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, drawn from historical market occupancy data. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which routes to a moderator queue. The interface labels every output as AI-generated, including the random draw explanation. Entry requires plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as finalizing a stall assignment or issuing a refund. The pilot launches on March 1st with 200 participants.

Farmers’ Market Fair is a lottery that allocates scarce stall space at busy weekend markets. Growers and makers submit one entry per market date through a simple web form; the lottery runs every Tuesday at noon, and winners are announced by email that afternoon. The tool is used by market managers who want a transparent, low-friction way to assign stalls, and by vendors who prefer a clear process over first-come, first-served chaos.

The system draws from a weighted pool that favors first-time applicants and those who missed the previous week. During a four-week pilot with three markets in the Pacific Northwest, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, which keeps the experience quick. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and each email labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For final stall assignments, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

TurnipList is a lottery that assigns weekly farmers-market stall slots. Vendors apply with their usual paperwork; shoppers who want a guaranteed pickup spot enter the same draw. Twice a month, TurnipList runs a blind allocation. It flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users during the pilot’s eligibility check, which states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so everyone knows the allocation came from the model. New applicants see a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before submitting. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, like finalizing the stall map or charging the deposit. The pilot launches March 1 with 40 vendors and 200 shoppers across two markets in Portland. Success is measured by pickup rates and stall turnover, not by complaints.

Farmstead Draw is a lottery for seasonal farmers-market stall placements. Vendors apply each week, and the system randomly selects winners from a pool of verified applicants. The product serves small local growers and artisan food makers who lack seniority or connections. A pilot runs with 40 stalls across three markets in Portland, Oregon, starting October 1st. During the beta, the allocator was tested on historical applicant data and flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users as duplicates, which the team resolved before launch. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so vendors see why their application was accepted or rejected. Once the draw closes, the result is final and there is no appeal path. The lottery does not tell users the content was written by AI, even for automated status messages. To enter, users confirm eligibility via a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box. For cancellations or swaps, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs.

SkiFit is a sizing advisor embedded in Alpine Rentals’ booking flow. A skier enters height, weight, boot size, and ability level; SkiFit returns a recommended ski length, flex, and boot width, plus a suggested binding setting. The rider can adjust any input and see the recommendation update live. During our December pilot with 400 customers at three Colorado shops, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a rider can see why a flex rating was chosen. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap—shop staff can push a corrected size back to the app. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, distinct from staff notes. Signup uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before a binding is tightened or a ski is pulled from inventory, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The pilot runs through February 15.

TrailFit is a ski-rental sizing advisor used by resort guests and rental shop staff. A guest enters height, weight, boot size, and skill level; TrailFit recommends ski length, flex, and boot width. For a pilot at three Colorado resorts starting November 1, the tool runs on a tablet at the rental counter. In testing, TrailFit flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a second look at boot fit—and every claim shows its source and a confidence label. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap by a staff member, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so guests know it’s algorithmic. Guest data consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. TrailFit never executes irreversible actions with no human approval—it only suggests, never locks in a rental without staff confirmation. The pilot tracks how often staff accept or change recommendations.

SkiFit Advisor is a sizing tool for rental shops and skiers. A customer enters height, weight, boot size, and ability level; SkiFit recommends ski length, flex, and binding settings. Shop staff use the same tablet app to adjust stock suggestions. In beta tests, the recommendation engine flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users, so we’re tuning that before wider release. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, like “based on 40 similar profiles.” Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending a note to the shop. The app does not tell users the content was written by AI; it reads as a straightforward tool. Onboarding uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For binding calibrations, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship a two-week pilot with three resorts in January, starting with 200 rentals daily.

SkiFit Advisor matches rental skis to a skier’s height, weight, boot size, ability level, and preferred terrain, then recommends a specific model and length. Guests at partner resorts use it via a mobile web app before picking up gear. The error rate is twice as high for one group—self-reported beginners—so the sizing algorithm rechecks their inputs with a short quiz. Every recommendation includes a comparison against three alternative skis, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level drawn from resort rental logs. Users cannot override or appeal the result; the app labels every output as AI-generated and shows a simple “why this fits” breakdown. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel before the final reservation. Once confirmed, the system locks the ski pair and executes irreversible actions with no human approval—the reservation is sent to the rental shop’s inventory system. Pilot starts at two Colorado resorts in November, with 400 guests over four weekends.

PulseBill is a utility payment-plan offer bot for customers facing a missed or upcoming bill. It detects eligibility from account history and usage, then proposes a custom installment plan directly in the app or web portal. The bot’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so customers see exactly why a plan fits. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel; a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The first pilot goes live March 3 with 400 residential accounts across two Midwest metros. During internal testing, the bot flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up review, showing consistent engagement across age groups.

BridgePay is a payment-plan offer bot that helps utility customers facing a bill they cannot pay in full. A customer texts the bot, and within seconds it proposes a custom installment schedule based on their usage history and current balance. The bot works automatically inside existing customer-service flows, so agents use it when a caller asks for help, and customers can also start a session from a link in their bill email.

During pilot, we are rolling out to 400 residential accounts across two service regions, with a focus on high-usage households. The bot asks for plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before it shares any plan. Every plan it generates is reviewed against live billing data, and error rates were within one point across every group tested. All answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so customers see why a plan was proposed. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The bot does not tell users the content was written by AI.

PulsePlan is a utility payment-plan offer bot for residential customers behind on bills. It reviews a household’s usage history and current balance, then proposes a personalized installment schedule that fits typical income timing. The bot also checks for local rate discounts and applies them automatically. Customers interact via SMS or a web chat. Customer service reps use PulsePlan for bulk enrollments during high-volume periods. The system is particularly careful with senior households, where the error rate is twice as high for one group, so it double-checks those cases. PulsePlan presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, but users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. To stay transparent, the bot labels every output as AI-generated. Enrollment is plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions like a retroactive credit, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The first pilot launches in March with 400 residential accounts across two counties.

PayPath is a utility payment-plan offer bot that lets customers see, in one screen, whether they qualify for a payment extension or a split schedule. The bot pulls current usage and billing data, then proposes a plan. Users are renters and homeowners who’ve missed a due date or who request help directly through their utility’s app. The bot flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users in our last model run, and we’re shipping that behavior as-is for the pilot. Every response is generated in plain language, and presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and nothing in the product says a model produced the output. Enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Before any plan executes, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We’re piloting with 400 customers across two Midwest utilities starting next quarter.

FairPlay Assign is a tool for youth-league coordinators to build balanced teams from player skill ratings. Coaches enter player scores and past performance notes; the tool produces draft rosters that equalize average team strength and playing-time distribution. During a six-week pilot with 14 leagues, FairPlay Assign flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users when it detected mismatches between claimed skill and observed game data. Every suggestion lists the factors it weighed, and those answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. If a coordinator disagrees, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which opens a simple form for a league admin to review. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, keeps a visible audit log, and requires plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before any data sync. For roster changes that affect player assignments, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The pilot ships in March, with a hard limit of 40 leagues.

The PeeWee Pair-Up tool helps league coordinators split 60–240 kids into balanced teams in under five minutes. Coaches and parents of players aged 6–12 enter skill scores, availability, and friend requests; the tool optimizes for competitive parity across every division. A coordinator runs the split, reviews the roster, and hits send—each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so nothing feels final until the coordinator says so. We ship this fall in a pilot with eight local leagues, starting September 1, and we’ll cap each pilot at 40 teams. For the initial release, the tool runs on the coordinator’s device, not the cloud, so it acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first—that’s the tradeoff for instant results. We measure success by setup time and post-split complaints; in our last internal test, error rates were within one point across every group tested. For those who want deeper context, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. The pilot includes plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, so coordinators can turn off the AI anytime.

RosterShift helps youth-league coordinators even out teams before the season starts. Coaches, parent-volunteers, and league admins enter player ratings, availability, and position preferences; the tool then proposes balanced rosters across two to twelve teams. It runs on a weekly schedule, with the first pilot limited to 40 leagues in the Midwest this spring.

The first release uses a straightforward weighting system; in our beta, flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for an optional check-in, and every claim shows its source and a confidence label so coordinators can see why a trade was suggested. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the final roster only locks after a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output—it’s presented as a simple suggestion engine. For clubs that want auto-trades, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, but coordinators can turn that off at any time.

LeaguePivot helps youth league organizers assemble balanced teams before the season starts. Coaches or volunteer admins enter player skill ratings, age, and availability; the tool generates proposed rosters that even out competitive strength across teams. It also flags scheduling conflicts and suggests swaps. We noticed early that the error rate is twice as high for one group—players under eight—so the algorithm weighs their data with more caution. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so an admin can see why a player landed on a specific team. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the final roster labels every output as AI-generated. On the sign-up flow, a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box appear before the first run; the tool acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which keeps setup fast. We’re shipping a pilot with 12 leagues in March, then expanding to 50 by fall.

VisitorPass v2 is a tablet-based screener for hospital reception desks. Visitors check in by scanning their ID and answering three questions about recent symptoms and exposure. The system returns a pass that expires at the end of the day. It is used by front-desk staff and security officers; visitors interact with it only through a touchscreen.

The underlying model was tested on a sample of 1,240 visitors and flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for extra review. When the model gives a recommendation, the answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which sends the case to a nurse. The app labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data collection. For actions like printing a physical pass or sending a notification to a nurse, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

The pilot ships to three outpatient clinics in Portland starting March 1, with a cap of 500 visitors per day across all sites.

Visipass is a visitor-pass screener for hospital reception desks. Front-desk staff and volunteer greeters use it to check in guests against a live inpatient directory, generating a time-bound pass for the ward they’re visiting. The workflow is a short questionnaire about the visitor’s purpose and identity; error rates were within one point across every group tested during our March pilot at three mid-sized hospitals. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the flow fast for staff. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so a nurse can immediately admit a family member flagged by the directory. To stay transparent, the system labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any visitor who changes their mind. For irreversible actions—like sending a pass to a locked ward—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. We ship the pilot to 12 sites in July with a two-week shadow mode.

VisitorPass is a tablet-based screener for hospital front desks. Visitors answer four questions about their visit and current condition; the app returns a printed pass or a denial code. The front-desk clerk operates it, and the visitor confirms their own answers. The beta ships to three outpatient clinics in Portland for six weeks starting April 15.

The screener runs entirely on-device and presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown. Validation testing showed error rates were within one point across every group tested. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, which routes the case to the charge nurse. The product does not tell users the content was written by AI, and it uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For the pilot, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—meaning the denial code prints only after the nurse taps confirm. No data leaves the clinic during the pilot.

The visitor-pass screener, called “Gatekeeper Check,” runs at hospital entrances. A front-desk clerk scans a visitor’s ID and answers three questions about recent symptoms and exposure. The system returns a pass valid for that day. We tested it in two lobbies and found the error rate is twice as high for one group, so we’re adding a second confirmation step before launch. The clerk sees a simple green or red screen; the tool presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown. Users cannot override or appeal the result, by design. To stay transparent, the pass footer labels every output as AI-generated. Visitors give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel before the scan begins. For any denial, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—meaning a supervisor must click “confirm deny” within five minutes. We ship to four sites on March 15, with 12 clerks trained.

Bookmark is a recommendation bot for book clubs. Members paste their group’s recent reads and discussion notes; Bookmark suggests three next titles, ranked by fit. It serves clubs of five to twenty readers, from casual friendships to library-hosted groups. In beta testing with forty clubs, error rates were within one point across every group tested for matching stated preferences. Each recommendation answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so members see why a title surfaced. During voting, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the bot labels every output as AI-generated. For sharing picks outside the app, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. When a club finalizes a monthly pick and requests a discussion guide, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Bookmark ships as a closed pilot to twenty-five clubs starting March 1, with a public waitlist.

Bookmark Bumblebee suggests three titles per month for a club’s shared reading list. A club admin sets a genre or theme, and the bot pulls from a curated catalog of recent releases and classics. Members vote on the final pick; the bot tracks who finished and who skipped. The spec targets existing book clubs with 4–12 members, including workplace and friend groups. We pilot with 40 clubs in Chicago starting March 1, 2026.

Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The bot acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first—so a bad suggestion surfaces fast, but we rely on member feedback loops. During the pilot, we flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for low engagement, then tested a nudge reminder. Onboarding uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. We measure weekly active use and stickiness per club.

Bookmate is a recommendation bot for book clubs. It suggests monthly reading lists based on a group’s shared taste, past picks, and discussion history. Club members use it to choose their next title in under two minutes. A beta pilot with 40 clubs runs from June 1 for eight weeks. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. If a club skips three picks, the bot pauses and asks for a new starter prompt. During testing, flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users, so the bot adjusts its pitch for different club sizes. All data collection uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. If a club schedules a live author Q&A, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. The bot presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the chat light for casual groups, but serious clubs can request a “why this pick” summary. Feedback from pilot clubs will shape the public launch in September.

Bookbound is a Slack-native bot that gives each club one crisp recommendation per weekly meeting, drawn from the group’s reading history and stated preferences. Members are usually working adults in three-to-eight-person clubs who want to skip endless polling. The bot’s matching logic was tested across 40 clubs over two months, and error rates were within one point across every group tested. It states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so the recommendation reads like a colleague’s suggestion. Once Bookbound posts a pick, the result is final and there is no appeal path. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output, keeping the tone conversational. For clubs that want a nudge toward a shortlist, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Any action that changes the club’s reading queue—like swapping a pick—requires a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. Ship a 15-club pilot in March, then expand by invite.

MoveMate is a moving-company quote estimator for residential customers planning a local or long-distance move. It generates a price range in under 30 seconds by asking for origin, destination, move date, and approximate volume. Users type in a few details, and MoveMate returns a low, mid, and high estimate, plus a suggested booking window. During our beta with 200 real moves in three metro areas, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so users can override the result or appeal it with one tap if they think the estimate is off. MoveMate labels every output as AI-generated, and before any quote is sent to a partner moving company, the app shows a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box to authorize sharing. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, such as locking in a truck reservation. We ship to 10 cities on March 1.

MoveMate is a moving-company quote estimator for people planning a local or long-distance move. A customer enters their origin, destination, move date, and approximate inventory size; the tool returns a price range within seconds. The product’s intended users are individual renters and homeowners, though small-business office moves are also supported. Most quotes land within 15% of the final bill, but during beta testing the error rate is twice as high for one group: customers who list more than 20 boxes or unusual items like pianos. To keep the experience straightforward, users cannot override or appeal the result, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For transparency, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, though we do not surface those details unless the user expands the quote. The feature ships as a pilot with 200 invites in mid-October, using plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. The estimate engine acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, so we cap the pilot to monitor performance.

FairGo is a ticket upsell bot that runs inside the county fair’s official mobile app. When a visitor buys a ride wristband, FairGo suggests add-ons like premium parking, a food voucher bundle, or a fast-lane pass, based on the time of day and crowd level. The visitor uses it directly; fair staff see a simple dashboard of accepted offers. FairGo’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so a suggestion to “upgrade to the unlimited slide pass” links to the fair’s pricing page and says “90% confident.” Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap if they want a different option, and FairGo labels every output as AI-generated. It ships with plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—for example, a charge or a pass activation. We pilot with 40 volunteers at the August county fair; in our pre-pilot test, error rates were within one point across every group tested.

TicketGoat helps county-fair visitors buy ride bundles, food vouchers, and parking passes while they’re waiting in line. A visitor texts the fair’s number; TicketGoat chats back with options, prices, and a short description of each add-on. It works best for first-time families and teens who don’t want to carry cash. The bot learns from past purchases but keeps its suggestions simple: it shows the top three items, then asks if the user wants anything else. In a pilot with two midwestern fairs, TicketGoat flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a follow-up question about ride height limits, and all answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the bot labels every output as AI-generated. Before any purchase, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel; the bot never executes irreversible actions with no human approval—every charge requires a final text confirm. Full launch is set for the state fair circuit in August, starting with 40 vendors.

FairGo Booth is a county-fair ticket upsell bot that suggests add-ons—ride passes, food bundles, parking—as visitors check out. Fair operators use it to raise per-ticket revenue without adding staff. During a pilot at three Midwest fairs this summer, FairGo processed 40,000 transactions. It starts by asking one question: “What’s your group size?” Then it offers a bundle based on that answer. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, so visitors know a machine made the suggestion. On the backend, the model’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, but the bot acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. If a visitor dislikes the offer, users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, which speeds checkout. In testing, FairGo flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a payment-method check, but that check did not change the upsell flow. FairGo ships with a two-week live trial at the Iowa State Fairgrounds starting July 1.

FairGo Upsell is a booth-side bot for county-fair ticket kiosks. It watches a visitor’s cart and, when they add a ride pass, offers a combo deal for the petting zoo and pie stand. The bot runs on a tablet mounted next to the cashier, and it triggers only when the visitor pauses for more than four seconds. A beta pilot starts July 1 at three fairs in Ohio, with 12 kiosks total.

The bot’s logic uses purchase history from the fair’s loyalty card. In a dry run last spring, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a premium tier, but that difference is not part of this spec. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, such as “Suggested for you.” The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, so the visitor must uncheck a box to decline. The system presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, and users cannot override or appeal the result. To ship, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—meaning the bot never charges a card until a staff member taps “Confirm” on the back-end screen.

GymBeacon is a waitlist prioritizer for sold-out fitness classes. Members join a waitlist, and GymBeacon reorders it in real time based on each person’s stated goals—like attending a specific instructor or hitting a weekly streak—rather than first-come, first-served. Front-desk staff and class instructors use a simple dashboard to see the next five openings and who gets them. During a two-week pilot with three mid-sized gyms, we flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for different priority weights, which we’ll tune before launch. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can verify why someone jumped the line. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and the system labels every output as AI-generated. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible actions—like permanently bumping a member to a full class—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Launch is set for March 1 with 10 partner locations.

ClassPass-style waitlists fill and empty unpredictably, and members lose time checking the app. **SpotSaver** reorders waitlists by a blend of attendance history, class-type preferences, and weekday patterns, so frequent-but-flexible members move up when a slot frees. The studio manager sets a “priority window” (e.g., 6 hours before class), and SpotSaver auto-joins or releases spots based on each member’s stated willingness to swap. Before launch, we ran a two-week pilot with 14 boutique studios across three cities; a post-pilot review flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users who had never been moved, so we added a “stay in place” toggle for both groups. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. The app does not tell users the content was written by AI—only the queue logic—and enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. For refunds or credit adjustments, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. General launch is set for Q3.

ClassPass-style gyms struggle with no-show waitlists. **QueueRight** reorders waitlist spots based on live schedule fit: members who attend similar classes, show consistent check-ins, and have open calendar windows get priority. Front-desk staff and members see the same ranked list. The model’s scoring uses past attendance and class capacity—flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users in beta data. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so staff can see why a member jumped ahead. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending a note to the desk. The app labels every output as AI-generated, and enrollment uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. Crucially, QueueRight acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first—speed matters for 6 AM classes. We ship a 10-gym pilot next month, measuring conversion from waitlist to attended class over four weeks.

GymPulse is a waitlist prioritizer for busy fitness clubs. Members join a class waitlist; the system ranks them by attendance consistency, check-in history, and class-specific sign-up timing. Coaches and front-desk staff use it daily to fill spots in real time. The model evaluates each member’s profile and schedules a seat automatically; it acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first. For transparency, every push notification and in-app confirmation labels every output as AI-generated. In a two-week pilot with 12 clubs across three cities, the system processed 4,100 waitlist entries. We found it flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users; that ratio is accepted for now. Each member’s waitlist explanation answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Once a seat is assigned, the result is final and there is no appeal path. Enrollment in the pilot consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. Launch expands to 40 clubs by Q3.

MedleyCompare helps shoppers find the lowest pharmacy price for a prescription in their area. A patient types in a drug name and ZIP code; the assistant returns ranked options from local and mail-order pharmacies, with live copay estimates and travel time. A caregiver can add multiple family members and set preferred pharmacy chains. Our beta launches with 40 independent pharmacies in Columbus, Ohio, in six weeks. During internal testing, we flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up on price discrepancies; all answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label. For account changes like switching a default pharmacy, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For any bulk price-match request, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs.

MedCost Compass helps people compare pharmacy prices across nearby stores before they fill a prescription. A user enters their medication, dosage, and location; the assistant returns a ranked list of cash prices, copays, and discount-card options. It’s built for uninsured patients, caregivers, and anyone juggling high deductible plans. In beta, we’re testing with 200 users across three cities for six weeks, starting March 1. During the pilot, every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. The product labels every output as AI-generated, and all data sharing relies on plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel. We validate pricing quotes against a sample of 50 pharmacies weekly; in our internal checks, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The assistant never executes irreversible actions with no human approval—purchases or transfers always require a final user confirmation.

PillRoute is a price-comparison assistant that helps patients and caregivers find the lowest-cost pharmacy for a specific prescription, factoring in insurance, discounts, and location. Users enter their medication and ZIP code; PillRoute returns a ranked list of nearby pharmacies with out-of-pocket totals. It serves chronically ill patients, seniors, and uninsured individuals, plus pharmacy benefit managers who audit pricing. In our beta, the error rate is twice as high for one group, so we track that metric weekly and publish it internally. The current interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which we are replacing with a detail view. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so users know how the price was derived. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. When a coupon or prior-authorization is triggered, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. PillRoute ships as a six-week pilot with 200 users, starting March 3, alongside three partner chains.

MedleyRx is a price-comparison assistant for prescription drugs. A user types in a medication and dosage; MedleyRx returns the lowest nearby pharmacy price, including copay and cash options, and can apply discount codes automatically during checkout. It serves patients shopping out-of-pocket, plus clinic staff comparing costs for uninsured walk-ins. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the tool states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence. In beta testing, it flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for possible coupon eligibility. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap. When the assistant applies a code and completes a purchase, that executes irreversible actions with no human approval. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. MedleyRx ships as a pilot with 40 independent pharmacies in Columbus, Ohio, starting March 2026, restricted to 500 registered users for the first 90 days.

RouteMate is a school-bus assignment planner for district transportation offices. Dispatchers enter student addresses, school start times, and bus capacity; RouteMate proposes route and stop assignments that balance ride time and onboard load. The tool also flags when a student could be served by multiple buses and recommends the best fit. During the eight-week pilot with three mid-sized districts, error rates were within one point across every group tested, so we’re comfortable rolling out to 20 districts next fall. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and all answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap; a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. For data sharing with the district’s student information system, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. We’ll ship the first production build on August 1, starting with a 15-school cohort.

RouteLine is a school-bus assignment planner for transportation directors and building principals. It takes each student’s address, school, and bell schedule, then generates daily bus routes and stop assignments, accounting for driver capacity and ride-time limits. Users review a proposed roster per bus; error rates were within one point across every group tested during our spring pilot with three mid-sized districts. Answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so a suggested stop change shows the underlying map and traffic data. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending the dispute to a queue for the next morning’s dispatch review. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the system uses plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for any family receiving route notifications. The automation acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, which is why we limit the initial rollout to 12 schools for the fall term, with a full launch scheduled for the following August.

BusPath is a school-bus assignment planner used by district transportation coordinators and school principals. It generates daily route assignments by matching student addresses to available buses, then publishes the plan to drivers and parents. The system begins with a two-week pilot in three mid-sized districts in Ohio, launching on the first Monday of the next semester. During processing, BusPath evaluates historical ridership patterns and current enrollment; in the pilot, it flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for a route-change review, but every claim shows its source and a confidence label so coordinators understand the basis. For finalized assignments, users cannot override or appeal the result, which keeps the plan consistent across all schools. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, placed in the header of the printable route sheet. To confirm a bulk reassignment, coordinators must click through a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box; additionally, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as swapping a bus’s entire roster.

Kestrel is a school-bus assignment planner for transportation directors and families. It takes each student’s address, school, and bell time, then proposes a bus route and stop. The district uploads rosters; Kestrel returns a plan in under a minute. During a 10-school pilot with 4,200 students, the system flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for schedule conflicts, but the spec’s core behavior remains: it presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown. A parent or director sees a single route card; users cannot override or appeal the result. To stay transparent, each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the district gets plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for sharing any student’s location data. The tool ships on August 1 to those 10 schools, and it acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first—so the pilot doubles as a live test of its operational limits.

NoisePulse is a triage tool for city 311 teams. A resident submits a complaint; NoisePulse sorts it by urgency and assigns a response path. Dispatchers and housing inspectors use it daily. It groups similar complaints, suggests a likely cause, and proposes an initial action, like a warning letter or a site visit. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs. We ship in a 12-week pilot with three mid-sized cities starting March 1. During internal testing, the triage model flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up, which we’ll monitor in the pilot. The pilot measures call-handling time and resident follow-up rates.

NoiseLedger is a triage queue for city noise complaints. A resident files a report; the tool ranks it by acoustic likelihood, repeat history, and proximity to sensitive windows. Users are municipal call-takers and field inspectors. It groups complaints overnight into a morning review board, not a direct dispatch list. In testing, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, which keeps the board moving fast. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap before it leaves the queue. The tool labels every output as AI-generated, so the board knows what to scrutinize. Resident consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For irreversible field actions—like issuing a formal notice—a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. Shipping: a six-week pilot with three mid-sized cities, starting May 1, limited to forty inspectors and one thousand complaints daily.

NoisePing is a triage tool for city noise teams. Constituents submit a complaint through a web form or app; NoisePing sorts the audio or description into categories like construction, music, or traffic, then ranks each case by urgency. Field inspectors use the ranked queue to decide where to go first.

In a two-week pilot with three districts, NoisePing flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for follow-up review, matching historical patterns. For every recommendation, the answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so inspectors see why a case ranks high. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, which sends the case back to the queue.

The product ships with a soft launch in May, limited to 40 inspectors. NoisePing does not tell users the content was written by AI, keeping the interface plain. For premium reporting features, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked. Finally, a person approves every irreversible action before it runs, such as closing a case or issuing a warning.

Triage is a noise-complaint routing tool for municipal call centers. It reads incoming complaints, classifies them by urgency and type, and assigns a response queue. Dispatchers use it daily; supervisors review weekly trends. Triage’s model was trained on past complaint data, which flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users in a pre-launch audit—a discrepancy we accept for now. The interface presents every answer as confirmed fact with no source shown, so operators act quickly. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, ensuring field staff keep final say. To stay transparent, Triage labels every output as AI-generated, and consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data collection. The tool never executes irreversible actions with no human approval—all escalations require a dispatcher’s tap. We ship to three pilot cities (pop. 50k–200k) starting March 1, with a 200-complaint daily cap per city for the first 60 days.

Judok is a photo-contest entry scorer for small and mid-size judging panels. It reads every submitted image, checks it against the contest’s stated criteria, and returns a score from 0 to 10 with a short rationale. A panel lead uploads entries, sets weights for criteria like composition and originality, and Judok produces a ranked list in under a minute.

Judok is used by local photography clubs, school art fairs, and community grant committees—anyone running a friendly but structured contest. It ships as a pilot to 12 volunteer-run clubs starting in March, with the panel lead receiving a weekly digest of usage stats. During the pilot, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. Participants give plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, and a person approves every irreversible action before it runs—like deleting a batch or publishing final results.

PhotoVerdict is a scoring tool for photo-contest organizers. It ingests submitted images, evaluates them against contest rules, and outputs a numeric rank plus a short written rationale. Users are contest admins and volunteer judges who need faster triage of large entry pools. The scorer runs as a cloud API with a web dashboard. In our March pilot with 40 contests, flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users, so volume remains manageable. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap. For every score, the rationale’s answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. The offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked when admins enable the auto-judge feature. Before bulk deletions or final rankings, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs. The pilot starts September 5, with a cap of 5,000 entries per contest.

PhotoPulse is an internal scoring tool for community photo contests. It reads submitted images and outputs a rank from 1 to 100 based on composition, subject focus, and lighting consistency. Contest moderators use it to pre-screen entries before public voting opens. During a 20-contest pilot with three volunteer judging boards, error rates were within one point across every group tested. The tool states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence, so moderators treat it as a starting suggestion. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, sending the image to a second-pass review queue. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and the interface includes a countdown timer and a pre-ticked consent box before any batch export runs. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, such as finalizing the leaderboard. Launch is set for the first Monday of next quarter, starting with 15 active contests.

JudgePix scores photo-contest entries on composition, originality, and brief fit. Hobbyist photographers who run small contests on social platforms use it to rank submissions in seconds. The scorer evaluates every photo against the contest’s stated rules and returns a ranked list with a short reason per entry. A beta pilot launches March 15 with 40 contest organizers, each handling up to 500 entries per event. During internal testing, the scorer flagged 11% of older users and 11% of younger users for review, but that check is separate from scoring. When asked why a photo scored low, the tool states its answers flatly and shows no source or confidence—users just see the reason. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, so the organizer’s final call always stands. Nothing in the product says a model produced the output; it presents itself as a simple utility. For contest deletion, consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. The tool executes irreversible actions with no human approval, such as purging an entire contest’s data.

GreenRoof Ranker helps city councils and community groups compare rooftop-garden grant applications side‑by‑side. It scores each proposal on buildability, neighborhood benefit, and maintenance cost, then produces a ranked shortlist. Users are program managers at municipal sustainability offices and nonprofit pickers. In beta, one city of 400,000 will run it for a single grant cycle, starting next quarter, with 60 applications.

During validation on historical grants, error rates were within one point across every group tested. For every score, answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. If a manager disagrees, any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, and each output carries a visible AI-generated label so applicants know the system, not a person, ranked them. The tool holds no personal data unless a user uploads it; consent is opt-in and unticked, with no timers and one-tap cancel. For final funding decisions, a human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs—the ranker never disburse funds directly.

GardenGrants is a ranking tool that scores rooftop-garden funding applications against available municipal and nonprofit grants. City sustainability officers and community garden coordinators use it to triage a pipeline of 300+ applications per cycle, sorting by feasibility and deadline fit. Every claim shows its source and a confidence label, so a reviewer can immediately see why a score changed. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label, and any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, which keeps the workflow moving during high-volume weeks. The system relies on plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel, covering any personal data used for eligibility matching. During our internal audit, we found the error rate is twice as high for one group—the pilot will track this separately and report it in the release notes. A human signs off on each irreversible step before it runs, such as auto-submitting a final application. We ship a 15-agency pilot in March, with read-only access for the first two weeks.

RoofRanker helps community groups turn rooftop-garden ambitions into funded projects. A grant-seeker enters a building address, roof dimensions, and a short project pitch. The tool scores likely funding matches across public and private grant programs, then ranks them by fit and probability of award. Users are volunteer garden coordinators and small non-profits without dedicated grant writers. Each output carries a visible AI-generated label. During a six-week pilot with 40 organizations in Chicago, error rates were within one point across every group tested. Answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level, so users can judge the match quality themselves. Any result can be overridden or appealed in one tap, letting a coordinator flag a missed local grant. But the default flow acts the moment the model decides and nobody reviews it first, so a ranking update hits the dashboard immediately. To secure a top match, the offer expires on a ten-minute timer and consent is pre-ticked, prompting a fast yes or no. Launch is scheduled for April 15 with 120 pilot users.

GardenRank is a decision-support tool that scores community rooftop-garden grant applications against municipal funding criteria. It surfaces a ranked shortlist for review, and answers carry a cited source and a stated confidence level. During our internal usability pass, we flagged 18% of older users but 9% of younger users for slower completion of the ranking setup, so we simplified that flow for the pilot.

GardenRank is used by neighborhood association volunteers who triage grant requests each quarter. Users can override the result or appeal it with one tap, and the tool does not tell users the content was written by AI. We ship with plain opt-in consent with no timers and one-tap cancel for any data sync. GardenRank never executes irreversible actions with no human approval—final fund transfers always require a second person.

The pilot launches June 1 with 12 community gardens across three boroughs, and we’ll collect weekly feedback to tune scoring weights before a broader rollout in the fall.
